title: Concept Drills — Chemistry of Metals (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Why does extracting a metal from its ore always require energy, and what decides WHICH reduction method is used?
questions.solution: Ores are the metal in OXIDISED form; reduction must reverse that, requiring electron supply — energy in some form. The method depends on the metal's position in the activity series: very reactive (Na, Al) need electrolysis; moderately reactive (Zn, Fe) need carbon reduction; least reactive (Ag, Au) need mere heating. Ease of reduction tracks reactivity.

questions.question: Why does aluminium reduce iron oxide (thermite) even though carbon is the usual reductant, and why is the reaction so vigorous?
questions.solution: Aluminium is MORE reactive than iron, so it displaces iron from its oxide: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. The reaction is violent because Al₂O₃ formation is hugely exothermic (Al's oxide bond is very strong) — the heat melts the iron produced. Reactivity difference + strong Al–O bond = self-sustaining high-temperature reduction.

questions.question: Why can't aluminium be extracted by carbon reduction, and why is cryolite added in the Hall–Héroult process?
questions.solution: Aluminium is too reactive: Al₂O₃ is so stable that carbon cannot reduce it economically (Al would reduce CO instead). Electrolysis of molten Al₂O₃ is required — but pure alumina melts at 2050 °C, impractically high. Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) dissolves Al₂O₃ and lowers the operating temperature to ~950 °C, cutting energy cost drastically. Reactivity → electrolysis; cryolite → feasibility.

questions.question: Why is rusting called 'reverse metallurgy', and why does painting prevent it?
questions.solution: Metallurgy reduces the ore to metal (energy in); corrosion re-oxidises the metal back toward its ore state (energy out) — the cycle reverses. Rusting needs BOTH oxygen and moisture (an electrolyte for the micro-galvanic cells). Painting excludes both, breaking the electrochemical circuit at the surface.

questions.question: Why is an alloy like bronze harder than either of its pure components?
questions.solution: Different-sized atoms of the alloying metal disturb the host lattice's regular packing, making layers harder to SLIDE over each other — the slip that makes pure metals soft is blocked. Hardness rises because deformation is obstructed, not because bonds are stronger. Alloying is lattice-level sabotage of slip.
